description: Somos un equipo joven hondureño apasionado por la ciencia, el espacio y la tecnología. Utilizamos datos de NASA, observación de la Tierra, inteligencia artificial e innovación para desarrollar soluciones a desafíos reales de Honduras.
summary:
In Honduras most farmers decide what to plant by gut feeling: what the father planted, what the neighbor says, what sold well last year. That knowledge is worth a lot, but it can't see a drought coming. AgroResilience is a tool that puts NASA data next to that experience. It does not decide for the farmer.

The core is an engine with two parts. Kharis, a small neural self made network trained on NASA POWER, IMERG, SMAP, GLDAS and GRACE, forecasts a year of daily weather for 30 points in the country and turns it into ten farm risks, like the canicula (mid-summer drought) or heat when the crop is flowering. Then a deterministic scoring engine uses the FAO-56 water balance to compare crop rotations and score each one from 0 to 100. Same data, same result, and every score says where it comes from and what we still don't know.
and a large language model generattes helpful explanations for farmers to understand why a rotation is better than other in plain english spanish or portuguese
details:
The problem: decisions by gut feeling

In Honduras, and in most of Central America, a small farmer decides what to plant by intuition. What the family has always planted, what the neighbor recommends, what sold well last season. That experience is real and we respect it, but it has a blind spot: it can not see a canicula (mid-summer drought) coming, or a heat wave right when the bean is flowering. In the Dry Corridor one of those can wipe out a full harvest.

AgroResilience is a decision-support tool, not a replacement for the farmer. It does not tell anyone what to do. It puts numbers from NASA next to what the farmer already knows, shows the risks of each option, and leaves the final decision with them.

How the engine works

The engine has two parts that run in a chain, and a language model that only explains the result.

1. Kharis, the forecast. Kharis is a lightweight neural network (a residual temporal convolutional network in PyTorch) that we trained on daily NASA POWER weather, GPM IMERG rain, SMAP soil moisture, GLDAS land data and GRACE water storage, plus ERA5 reanalysis to fill gaps. It covers 30 points across Honduras and forecasts 365 days of daily weather with an uncertainty band (p10, mean and p90). Then it turns that forecast into ten agronomic risk signals, P1 to P10, for example the canicula, long dry spells, waterlogging and heat during flowering. If the farmer shares GPS, we adjust the nearest point to the real altitude of the plot using SRTM terrain.

2. The decision engine. This part is deterministic: same data, same scores, every time. For each crop inside each rotation it does three things. First it calculates how much water the crop needs with the FAO-56 method (ET0 x Kc, split into the four crop stages). Second it counts the days above the crop heat limit during flowering. Third it compares effective rain, adjusted by how well the terrain holds water, against that need, and subtracts the canicula, dry spells and waterlogging.

With that it builds eight factors from 0 to 100: water, heat, sale, soil health, erosion control, pest break, natural nitrogen from legumes and forage. Each factor has a base weight, and every goal the farmer picks makes its factor weigh three times more. So two farmers on the same plot can get different rankings if they care about different things. There is also a safety rule: if the water score of any harvest falls below 30, the whole rotation is capped at 58, so the tool never recommends something that looks good on paper but dries out in the field.

3. The historical check. A separate module simulates every crop in every department from 1981 to 2026 with the WRSI water index and the FAO-33 yield response to water, grouped by El Nino phase. This lets the farmer see how a crop did in years that looked like this one. It matches the known bad years in the Dry Corridor.

4. The explanation. Only at the end, Google Gemini reads the scores and explains them in plain Spanish, English or Portuguese, and looks up regional market prices. It never changes a number.

What the farmer sees

Five questions: where, what terrain, what is planted now, what season and what matters most. The answer is the rotations ranked from best to worst, each with its score, how much better or worse it is than the current plan, how confident we are, the main reasons, the risks and what we still do not know. Every piece of evidence says which source it came from. We think being honest about uncertainty is what makes a farmer trust a tool, and also what keeps the tool from pretending to know more than the person who works the land.

How we built it

React, TypeScript, Vite and Leaflet for the web app, Capacitor for the Android app, Python and PyTorch for Kharis and the data pipeline, Supabase for the data and Vercel for hosting. The pipeline is one resumable command that downloads and processes only what is new. Almost every source is global, so with a new set of coordinates the same engine can run in another country.

Limits

It has not been tested with data from another country yet. The historical module catches the bad years, but its correlation with FAOSTAT yields is still low (r = 0.19 for maize, 0.02 for beans, 1981 to 2013). Some heat limits and crop coefficients are approximate, and the market index uses Honduran 2026 prices. That is one more reason the last word belongs to the farmer.

Live app: https://www.agroresilience.app
